result:
Both integrate changes from one branch into another; they differ in what they do to history.

**Merge** ties the two histories together with a new merge commit. Existing commits are untouched.

```
A---B---C  main
     \       \
      D---E---M  feature   (git merge main)
```

**Rebase** replays your commits on top of the other branch, creating new commits with new hashes. History becomes linear, as if you'd started your work from the latest tip.

```
A---B---C  main
         \
          D'---E'  feature   (git rebase main)
```

| | Merge | Rebase |
|---|---|---|
| History | Preserves what actually happened, with branch points | Linear, rewritten |
| Commits | Adds one merge commit | Replaces yours with new copies |
| Conflicts | Resolved once, in the merge commit | Resolved per replayed commit |
| Safe on shared branches | Yes | No, since it rewrites hashes others may have based work on |
| Undo | `git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD` or revert the merge commit | `git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD` or use `git reflog` |

**Rule of thumb:** rebase your own local, unpushed work to tidy it up on top of the latest `main`; merge when integrating into shared branches. Never rebase commits that others have already pulled, because it forces a force-push and leaves everyone else with diverged history.

A common workflow combines both: `git rebase main` on your feature branch to get up to date, then merge the feature into `main` (optionally with `--no-ff` to keep a visible merge commit).
